svg.aria-label: An engineering figure on diaphragm mass lumping in ETABS. Left: a floor plan meshed into nodes, each carrying a tributary mass. Nodes on the assigned diaphragm lump their mass to the diaphragm master node, shown by converging arrows, so the storey mass equals the sum of the assigned tributary masses. A late-drawn unassigned patch has nodes that do not lump, so their mass is excluded. Right: the consequence chain as a full-versus-leaked comparison with formulas. The storey mass drops, so the auto storey force, which is the design coefficient times the mass, drops in proportion, and the accidental torsion, which is the storey force times 0.1b, drops as well, while the centre of mass shifts. Bottom: a rigid diaphragm assigned to the area object lumps every meshed node to the master, whereas one assigned only to the corner points leaves the interior nodes unlumped.
svg.text: How a Missing Diaphragm Leaks Mass Out of the Seismic Load
Storey mass is the sum of what lumps to the diaphragm master. What isn't assigned isn't counted.
A. How ETABS builds the storey mass
each cell = tributary mass m at its node
nodes do not lump: m(i) excluded
M(storey) = Σ m(i) over assigned nodes only. Hatched m(i) never enter the sum.
B. What that does to the load (full vs leaked)
the hatched patch simply isn't in the sum
Auto storey force F = Cd · M
force scales with mass: the floor is under-loaded
and the CM shifts: corner elements get less torsion than the code requires
C. The subtle version: where the rigid diaphragm is assigned decides which nodes lump
Assigned to the corner POINTS only
The storey mass is only what lumps to the master. Everything downstream scales with it.
Read the storey mass table against floor area × unit loads. A shortfall on one storey is a diaphragm problem on that storey.
